items.answerRationale: Nobody is a singular indefinite pronoun, so knows agrees with it. Each, someone, and anybody are also singular; have, are, and need respectively fail to agree with those subjects.
items.rule: Singular indefinite pronouns take singular present-tense verbs, regardless of intervening or nearby words.

choicePairs.reason: Both are singular indefinite subjects followed by a plural noun and an incorrectly plural verb; the of-phrase versus locative phrase changes the wording more than the agreement task.
Each of the markers and nobody among the volunteers both require a singular verb despite a nearby plural noun; correctness differs, but the subject-identification rule is the same.
A places a plural noun after the indefinite subject, while D uses a participial modifier without a competing plural noun. D is structurally simpler.
Both use a singular indefinite subject plus a prepositional phrase containing a plural noun; they differ mainly in vocabulary and verb correctness.
B has a plural-noun prepositional phrase that could attract the verb; D has an arriving modifier and no plural-noun attraction.
C has an intervening plural noun in an among-phrase; D has a participial modifier and no plural-noun attraction.

items.distractorQuality: A and B are plausible agreement traps because plural nouns follow singular subjects. D is weaker because its singular subject has no competing plural noun. All three wrong choices repeat the same singular-indefinite-pronoun/plural-verb error, making elimination mechanical once that rule is recognized.

items.answerRationale: The singular head noun bundle agrees with rests. The plural directions requires explain; the singular key requires opens; the plural posters requires need.
items.rule: The present-tense verb agrees in number with the head of its subject, not with a noun in an intervening modifier.

choicePairs.reason: A has a plural head and an incorrectly singular verb after a participial modifier; B has a singular head, an of-phrase with a plural noun, and a correctly singular verb.
A is a plural-head/singular-verb error and C is a singular-head/plural-verb error; their intervening modifiers also differ.
Both are plural-head/singular-verb errors with an intervening singular noun. The participial phrase versus unlike-phrase changes syntax somewhat, but the agreement decision is effectively identical.
Both have a singular head followed by a prepositional phrase containing a plural noun. Only the chosen verb number changes the agreement result.
B tests a singular head against a nearby plural noun and agrees; D tests a plural head against a nearby singular noun and disagrees.
C incorrectly gives a singular head a plural verb, whereas D incorrectly gives a plural head a singular verb; the attraction direction reverses.

items.distractorQuality: A and D both plausibly draw attention to a nearby singular noun even though the head is plural; C reverses that attraction and is also plausible. The set offers both mismatch directions, but A/D and B/C form near-duplicate agreement decisions.

acrossItems.assessment: Both ask the learner to pick the sole complete sentence with correct present-tense agreement. In each, locate the subject head, ignore a nearby modifier, and choose the verb form that matches. Q01 narrows this to singular indefinite pronouns, while Q02 mixes singular and plural noun heads; the shared format and rapid elimination method still make the pair repetitive.
